title: Exodus Wilderness Routes and Water
aliases: Sea of Reeds and Sinai route debate
summary: A geography-focused evidence cluster that records the route and water markers named in Exodus and Numbers while treating modern identifications of the Sea crossing, Marah, Elim, Rephidim, and Mount Sinai as disputed reconstructions.
historical_context: Exodus and Numbers preserve ordered itineraries with named camps, wilderness zones, travel intervals, and water crises. Some eastern Delta place names are more securely discussed than later stations, but the complete route and the location of Mount Sinai remain disputed.
ancient_near_east_context: Movement through arid terrain is constrained by routes, drainage systems, grazing, and water availability. The narratives themselves repeatedly foreground these constraints; modern geographic models should be evaluated against the textual sequence without converting a proposed map into archaeological proof.
literary_context: Exodus 13-19 narrates the movement from Egypt to Sinai, while Numbers 33 presents a compressed station list. The two forms should be compared carefully because narrative episodes and itinerary notices provide different kinds of geographic detail.
covenantal_significance: The geographic evidence clarifies the narrative's route and resource pressures; it does not determine the theological meaning of the wilderness episodes or validate a single modern itinerary.
timeline: Exodus narrative setting: date and route reconstruction disputed
Exodus 13-19: narrative sequence from departure through the arrival at Sinai

Modern period: multiple competing identifications of the Sea crossing and Mount Sinai

interpretive_notes.note: The text's sequence of named stations is evidence; matching every name to a modern location is a separate and disputed reconstruction.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The literary itinerary is directly observable, whereas proposed site identifications depend on linguistic, archaeological, and geographic judgments.

interpretive_notes.note: Water scarcity is explicit in the narrative, but present-day springs or wadis should not be identified with Marah, Elim, or Rephidim without additional evidence.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The resource sequence is textual; the locations and degree of environmental continuity are not established by the names alone.

claims.claim: Exodus 13-14 names route choices and camps around the Sea crossing, but those textual markers do not by themselves settle the modern location of the crossing.
claims.rationale: The place names and sequence are explicit, while their mapping to modern geography remains disputed.
claims.notes: The claim does not select a Gulf, lake, lagoon, or canal-zone crossing.

claims.claim: Exodus 15 and Numbers 33 place a period without water before Marah and then describe Elim as a water-rich station.
claims.rationale: The sequence and contrasting water descriptions are direct textual features; modern site identification is excluded.
claims.notes: The claim does not identify a present-day spring or oasis.

claims.claim: Multiple scholarly routes can be proposed from the wilderness itineraries, but the intermediate stations and Mount Sinai cannot all be identified with consensus.
claims.rationale: The sources preserve route data but weigh place-name continuity, travel constraints, and archaeological evidence differently.
claims.notes: CKL records the disagreement instead of ranking modern Sinai candidates.

evidence_items.title: Sea crossing route markers and identification uncertainty
evidence_items.description: Exodus and Numbers preserve an ordered set of route choices and camp names around the Sea crossing, while modern geographic identifications remain contested.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The textual markers are explicit, but their modern locations and the precise body of water cannot be identified with sufficient consensus for a high-confidence reconstruction.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: This evidence keeps the narrative's actual geographic vocabulary in view and prevents a familiar modern map from being treated as the only route allowed by the passage.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Exodus 13-14 names a non-Philistine route, a wilderness direction, the Sea, Pi-hahiroth, Migdol, and Baal-zephon; Numbers 33 preserves a related station sequence.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Historical geographers disagree over the locations and over which eastern Egyptian or Sinai water system best fits the terminology and route sequence.

temporal_scope.notes: No modern route is promoted to contemporary archaeological evidence.

evidence_items.title: Marah and Elim water-station sequence
evidence_items.description: Exodus contrasts a three-day water shortage and undrinkable water at Marah with the springs and palms reported at Elim; Numbers 33 preserves the same station order.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The order and contrasting water descriptions are explicit in both itinerary contexts; the evidence item makes no modern site identification.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The sequence explains why water access is a concrete geographic constraint in the narrative rather than generic wilderness scenery.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The texts place Marah before Elim and contrast water scarcity or poor quality with a station characterized by multiple springs and palms.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Commentators treat the sequence as meaningful itinerary and resource information, while proposed matches with present-day springs remain uncertain.

evidence_items.title: Competing Sinai itinerary and mountain models
evidence_items.description: The combined Exodus and Numbers itineraries constrain proposed routes to Sinai but do not yield one consensus identification of all stations or of the mountain.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The texts provide ordered constraints, but uncertain place-name continuity and limited archaeological identification leave several materially different route models in scholarship.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: This item helps readers use itinerary evidence without treating a traditional or novel Mount Sinai candidate as an established fact of the passage.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Exodus places Rephidim before arrival in the wilderness of Sinai, and Numbers 33 supplies additional stations between the Sea and Sinai.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Davies, Hoffmeier, and other historical geographers weigh route directions, ancient place names, travel feasibility, and site evidence differently and do not produce a single consensus map.
